modules.label: About Sierra
modules.summary: Knowing Sierra's story, product, and culture cold is table stakes before either of these interviews.

lessons.title: Founding story
lessons.why: The founders' background explains a lot about how Sierra positions itself against both infra companies and legacy CX vendors.
facts: Bret Taylor left his role as co-CEO of Salesforce in January 2023; Clay Bavor left Google around the same time after 18 years there.
The two met working together at Google years earlier and decided to start Sierra together in 2023.
Sierra emerged from stealth on February 13, 2024, disclosing a $110M raise (Fortune exclusive).

lessons.title: Funding trajectory
lessons.why: The growth curve is part of the story — worth knowing the path, not just the current number.
facts: Valued at $1B at its February 2024 stealth launch, then $4.5B by October 2024 after raising $175M.
Reached a $10B valuation in September 2025 on a $350M raise.
Raised $950M in May 2026 at a $15.8B valuation, led by Tiger Global and Google's GV — one of the largest AI funding rounds of the year.
lessons.mustRemember: Cite the trajectory, not just the current number — interviewers reference the growth story.

lessons.title: What Sierra actually sells
lessons.why: The single most important framing to get right before either interview.
facts: Agent OS: one platform for building, deploying, and optimizing customer-facing AI agents across chat, voice, SMS, WhatsApp, email, and ChatGPT.
Sells to business/CX leaders making a platform decision, not primarily to developers integrating an API.
The pitch is a finished, branded agent for the customer's own brand — not raw infrastructure a developer builds on top of.

lessons.title: Notable customers
lessons.why: The customer list itself tells you Sierra isn't chasing one vertical.
facts: Retail/consumer: ADT, Sonos, WeightWatchers, Casper, The Gap.
Finance: Rocket Mortgage, SoFi.
Healthcare and telecom/other: Sutter Health, SoftBank.

modules.takeaway: Two ex-Big Tech operators building the operating system for customer-facing AI agents — stealth to $15.8B in under two and a half years.

modules.label: Agent OS: the Product
modules.summary: The specific modules and mechanics you'd actually be scoping and shipping in either role.

lessons.title: Agent Studio
lessons.why: The entry point for most non-engineering configuration work.
facts: A no-code builder for designing and configuring an agent's behavior.
Where most of the day-to-day scoping and iteration on an agent's conversational flow happens.
Built so business/CX teams can adjust agent behavior without needing an engineer for every change.

lessons.title: Agent SDK
lessons.why: The escape hatch when a customer's needs go beyond what the no-code builder supports.
facts: A developer toolkit for deeper customization than Agent Studio allows.
Used when an integration or behavior needs custom logic specific to a customer's systems.
This is where Agent Engineers spend most of their time — the boundary between Studio and SDK is a good line to know when scoping a project.

lessons.title: Voice
lessons.why: Sierra's phone-agent module — directly relevant given both roles sit inside an Agent Development team shipping voice and chat agents alike.
facts: Sierra added voice capabilities to its agents so they can handle phone calls, not just chat.
Built for natural, responsive conversation with seamless handoff to a human agent when needed.
Runs on the same underlying ASR/LLM/TTS building blocks covered in Voice AI Fundamentals — see the Landscape module here rather than re-deriving it.

lessons.title: Agent Data Platform (ADP)
lessons.why: One of Sierra's newest and most strategically important modules — persistent memory is a real differentiator versus a stateless chatbot.
facts: Launched November 2025 — gives agents persistent memory across sessions.
Gives an agent access to customer history, CRM records, real-time order status, and behavioral signals.
Unlike a stateless chatbot that starts every conversation from zero, an ADP-powered agent remembers the customer.

media.caption: Sierra CEO Bret Taylor on agents that have memory

lessons.title: Live Assist & Insights
lessons.why: The two modules that make an agent deployment operable day-to-day, not just demoable.
facts: Live Assist: a human-copilot mode where a live agent gets AI assistance mid-conversation, rather than the AI handling the call alone.
Insights 2.0: analytics for monitoring how agents are actually performing in production.
Both matter constantly in Agent Development work — this is how you and the customer know whether a shipped agent is actually working.

lessons.title: Trust & Reliability
lessons.why: Matters disproportionately given Sierra's customer list includes healthcare and finance.
facts: The security/guardrails module governing what an agent can and can't do or say.
A first-class concern for regulated-industry customers (healthcare, finance) where a wrong answer has real consequences.
Worth naming unprompted when discussing a hypothetical deployment for a regulated customer — it signals you're thinking past the demo.

modules.takeaway: The pitch in one line: reasoning, memory, channels, tooling, supervision, and analytics all live in one platform, not stitched together from point solutions.

modules.label: Agent Development: the Team & Roles
modules.summary: Agent Development is Sierra's forward-deployed team — Strategists, PMs, and Engineers embedded with customers to actually ship agents, not just sell them.

lessons.title: What the Agent Development team does
lessons.why: The team both linked roles sit on — worth understanding as a unit before the individual role breakdowns.
facts: A forward-deployed team, embedded with a customer's engineering, CX, or operations teams depending on their needs.
Has supported hundreds of deployments — the team's whole reason to exist is the gap between a good demo and an agent that holds up across millions of real conversations.
Success is measured in customer outcomes: higher CSAT, lower churn, stronger brand, increased revenue, better margins — not in shipping features for their own sake.

lessons.title: Strategist, Agent Development — the role
lessons.why: One of the two roles directly linked — worth having this cold, not paraphrased.
facts: Partners with Agent Product Managers and Agent Engineers to scope, build, and ship agents handling thousands of conversations a day.
Combines product strategy, conversational design, and customer insight — acts as a trusted advisor driving the customer's own AI strategy.
Drives execution and delivery of multiple complex, high-visibility projects, coordinating technical and non-technical stakeholders through the full development lifecycle.

lessons.title: Product Manager, Agent Development (APAC) — the role
lessons.why: The second linked role — note this specific posting is for one of Sierra's first Agent PMs on a brand-new regional team.
facts: One of Sierra's first Agent PMs, joining the founding APAC team.
Partners directly with engineers and customers — engaging stakeholders up to executive level to discover requirements, present demos, and work through technical challenges.
Expected background: 5-7+ years in product management of highly technical products, at or above Senior PM level.

lessons.title: Strategist vs. PM: how the two actually differ
lessons.why: Worth being able to articulate this distinction clearly — signals you understand the org, not just the two titles.
facts: Strategist leans toward consulting, go-to-market, and hands-on delivery execution across a portfolio of customer projects.
PM leans toward roadmap ownership, prioritization, and scoping which features actually get built, closer to a classic senior technical PM archetype.
Neither role writes the production agent code — that's the separate Agent Engineer track; both need enough technical fluency to work with engineers, not replace them.

modules.takeaway: Both roles are "sit with the customer and make the agent actually work," not "build the platform" — technical fluency is so you can talk to engineers, not replace them.

modules.label: Interview Prep
modules.summary: Sierra's interviews test whether you can design, ship, and reason about a production agent under real constraints — not trivia.

lessons.title: Sierra's interview philosophy
lessons.why: Sets expectations for the format you'll actually face, whichever role you're interviewing for.
facts: Sierra publicly rebuilt even its software-engineering interview away from algorithm trivia and toward representative, working-session-style formats.
The stated goal: test initiative, ownership, judgment, system understanding, and product thinking — the things the job actually requires day to day.
Expect a case- or working-session-style interview rather than a whiteboard puzzle, in either the Strategist or PM loop.

lessons.title: The Agent PM interview loop
lessons.why: The most concretely documented loop for either of the two linked roles — worth knowing the shape of it going in.
facts: Recruiter screen (~30 min): background, motivation to join Sierra, compensation expectations.
An unusually early technical filter: design an agentic AI support system.
A take-home prioritization case, then three final-round interviews — a case presentation plus live metrics case, a stakeholder-management round (really testing product sense), and a fit deep dive.

lessons.title: Q: Design an AI agent for a paying enterprise customer
lessons.why: A default prompt in the technical filter round — a strong structure matters more than any specific answer.
facts: Lead with the business outcome (containment, CSAT, revenue) before touching architecture.
Scope a narrow, high-confidence first use case rather than trying to "handle everything" on day one.
Name what data and system access the agent needs, how you'd validate it before going live, and how you'd measure success after launch.

lessons.title: Q: Prioritize a live agent roadmap under pressure
lessons.why: Tests judgment under a live-case format, not just a prepared framework.
facts: Anchor priority on customer-visible outcomes (containment, escalation rate) over internal engineering elegance.
Be explicit about the tradeoff — say plainly what you're consciously choosing not to do, and why.
Be ready to defend the call to a skeptical stakeholder in the room, not just state it once.

lessons.title: The stakeholder-management round: what it's really testing
lessons.why: Easy to underrate this round as "just behavioral" — it's actually core to the job.
facts: Because the role is forward-deployed and embedded, this round is testing whether you can hold a room with a frustrated customer executive and a skeptical engineer at the same time.
Bring a real example of navigating genuinely conflicting stakeholder asks under a deadline, not a clean hypothetical.
Framed by interviewers as a product-sense round in disguise — they're watching how you weigh competing asks, not just whether you're personable.

modules.takeaway: Every round comes back to one test: can you turn a real, messy customer problem into a scoped agent decision you can defend under questioning?

modules.label: Voice AI Landscape & Competitors
modules.summary: Sierra competes on being the full agent operating system, not raw model quality — knowing where the lines are drawn matters more than a feature checklist.

lessons.title: Where Sierra sits: applied platform, not infrastructure
lessons.why: The single clearest way to distinguish Sierra from a company like Deepgram in conversation.
facts: Sierra sells a finished, branded agent to business/CX buyers making a platform decision.
Infrastructure companies like Deepgram sell APIs/platforms to developers building their own agent on top.
See the Voice AI Fundamentals topic's Company Positioning module for the fuller Deepgram-vs-Sierra breakdown — same distinction, not repeated here.

lessons.title: Closest enterprise competitors: Decagon and Ada
lessons.why: The two names most likely to come up if asked "who competes with Sierra?"
facts: Current market analyses consistently name Decagon and Ada as the closest like-for-like enterprise agent platforms.
Like Sierra, both sell a finished, managed agent platform rather than raw model access.
Worth being able to name both without hesitation — not knowing your closest competitors reads poorly in either interview.

lessons.title: Helpdesk-native alternatives
lessons.why: The alternative path a prospective customer takes when they'd rather not adopt a separate platform.
facts: Intercom Fin and Zendesk's AI agents build the agent directly into a helpdesk the company already uses.
Gorgias plays a similar role specifically for Shopify-based e-commerce businesses.
This is the natural comparison when a prospective customer already has deep helpdesk lock-in.

lessons.title: Why companies actually switch away from Sierra
lessons.why: A more useful thing to know than any feature comparison — shows commercial fluency, not just product knowledge.
facts: Current market analyses point to cost and fit as the main reasons teams look elsewhere — not quality.
"Fit" usually means an existing helpdesk-native alternative is simply less disruptive to adopt.
Useful framing in an interview: naming this nuance signals you understand competitive dynamics, not just a feature list.

lessons.title: The voice AI stack underneath Sierra's Voice module
lessons.why: Ties this topic back to the underlying technology rather than treating Sierra's product as a black box.
facts: Sierra's Voice module runs on the same ASR / reasoning-layer / TTS building blocks covered in Voice AI Fundamentals.
The same cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech fork and latency-budget constraints apply — Sierra doesn't get a pass on physics.
See the Voice AI Fundamentals topic directly rather than duplicating that material here.

modules.takeaway: In a competitor conversation, naming the buyer difference (developer vs. business/CX buyer) lands sharper than naming a feature difference.
